block.label: READING · 48 HOURS IN BARCELONA
block.html:
Day 1. We arrived in Barcelona on a Friday morning and left our bags at the hotel. First, we walked down La Rambla, the most famous street in the city. It was crowded, but it was fun. Halfway down the street, we stopped at La Boqueria, a huge food market, and had fresh fruit juice for breakfast. In the afternoon, we visited Casa Batlló. People call it the "house of bones" because its balconies look like bones, and its roof looks like the back of a dragon. We booked our tickets online, so we didn't have to wait in the queue.

Day 2. On Saturday, we took the metro to Park Güell. Gaudí designed it as a place for rich families to live, but only two houses were sold, so the city opened it as a public park in 1926. The view of the city from the top is amazing. In the evening, we went to the beach. Before the 1992 Olympic Games, the city cleaned and rebuilt its beaches, and today they are full of people until late. We had dinner at ten o'clock, which is normal in Spain, and we watched the sunset first. It was the best day of the trip.

A made-up travel diary. The facts about the city are real.

block.label: READING 2 · SMALL PLATES, LATE DINNERS
block.html: In Spain, people often eat tapas: small plates of food that you share with friends. A typical night out is a "tapeo": you go from one bar to another and have one or two tapas in each place. Popular tapas include patatas bravas (fried potatoes with a spicy sauce), tortilla (a thick potato omelette) and croquetas. Meal times are late: lunch is usually around two or three o'clock, and dinner at nine or ten.
